asks.ans: Name the chain: Plex table → view → tile. Every teardown below prints it. If a tile has no Plex table, it is a manual input and the form is the source.

asks.ask: “Why do we need that at all?”
asks.ans: Because a tile on the scorecard reads it. If nothing reads it, we should not be building it — that is the honest answer, and it is worth saying.

Three different causes that look identical: the view was never created, the Plex tenant has no such data, or a filter can never match. Only the last is a bug, and it is the one that looks most like good news.

asks.ask: “Is this the same as the old number?”
asks.ans: Usually not, and usually on purpose. Say which definition changed. WIP fell 2.4× when the status filter was corrected — the new number is right.
Goals, safety incidents and turnaround standards: yes, through the manual-data form. Anything sourced from Plex: it changes in Plex, and the pipeline follows.
Overnight, on a schedule per pipeline. The Label Design queue is the exception — twice daily, at 10:00 and 14:00.

teardowns.q: How much did we actually ship and invoice this month?
teardowns.why: Revenue is counted when goods ship, not when an order is taken. That is why it comes from the Shipping module rather than the sales order. It reconciled exactly against 17 real carton records when shipments existed.
teardowns.watch: Reads 0 today because the test tenant holds no shipments at all. Every revenue view reads 0 together — that pattern is the signature of missing shipping data, not a broken view.

teardowns.q: At this pace, where does the month land?
teardowns.why: Straight-line projection: revenue so far ÷ days elapsed × days in month. Pure date maths on top of MTD Revenue — no new data.
teardowns.watch: Calendar days, not business days. A month that starts with a long weekend projects low.

teardowns.q: Are we on track against the revenue target?
teardowns.why: The goal side comes from the manual-data form (nobody can extract a negotiated target from an ERP). The v2_ prefix means it reads the resolver, which prefers a goal typed into the form and falls back to the spreadsheet — so the scorecard can move one tile at a time instead of all at once.
teardowns.watch: The revenue goals loaded are the company-wide SALES target. No revenue-specific goal exists anywhere in BigQuery. Revenue and Sales are deliberately different numbers, so this is a business assumption, stated on every row and retractable in one click.

teardowns.q: How much did we sell — orders taken, not goods shipped?
teardowns.why: A sale counts in the month its order first reached Pending Fulfillment, dated by that status change rather than by order entry. That is what makes it a different number from Revenue, on purpose — one measures selling, the other measures shipping.
teardowns.watch: Priced off the sales-order line price. It read $0 for weeks because it used the customer price list, and most parts have no list price.

teardowns.q: Is each rep on track?
teardowns.why: Rep goals and the company-wide target are maintained separately and are allowed to disagree — turnover means the eight reps sum to $4,690,000 against a $5,040,000 team goal. Team performance sums actuals, never goals.
teardowns.watch: scope is an exact string match on the rep name. A typo yields a NULL goal that reads as 0% forever with no error — which is why the form reads rep names from this very report instead of letting anyone type them.

teardowns.q: Which orders are sitting with accounting?
teardowns.why: Deposit Review is the accounting stage — confirmed 11 Sep. The full chain: Quote and Pending Sales Approval are internal sales stages; Deposit Review is accounting; once a payment is applied the order moves to Pending Fulfillment.
teardowns.watch: It was silently dead for weeks. It filtered Pending Payment Review, a status the September consolidation deleted, so it returned 0 rows — which reads exactly like “nothing is pending”. Now matched on the status name, never the numeric key.

teardowns.q: What have we sold that has not shipped yet?
teardowns.why: Exactly two statuses count: Pending Fulfillment and Hold. Held goods are still owed to a customer. It nets off any quantity already shipped, so a partly-shipped order contributes only its remaining balance.
teardowns.watch: The old filter (“not a quote, not cancelled”) also swept in Pending Sales Approval, Deposit Review and Closed, putting WIP at $43,723 against a true $17,950 — inflated 2.4×. Any screenshot from before 9 Sep overstates it.

teardowns.tile: Total in Shipping / Ready to Ship
teardowns.q: What is packed and waiting to go out the door?
teardowns.why: Counts only the ready quantity, never the whole order. Price falls back in order: shipment price → sales order line → customer list, and price_source records which was used, so an estimate is never mistaken for a real figure.
teardowns.watch: Shipper_Line.Price is 0 before a shipment is finalised on this tenant. Without the fallback this tile would read $0 while real goods sat on the dock.

teardowns.q: Which ingredients are we short of?
teardowns.why: Three conditions: the part number starts with 33, it has a minimum inventory quantity, and availability is negative. The 33 scan is name-based on purpose — a part-type dropdown was rejected because switching would break the rule. Demand includes what parent finished goods will consume via the bill of materials; without that no 33 part appears at all, because they have neither containers nor direct sales orders.
teardowns.watch: Proven 11 Sep with four real shortages, then back to 0 an hour later when those orders moved to Quote status. Both readings are correct — a quote is not demand. The field is Minimum_Inventory_Quantity; a part with 0 is treated as “no threshold set” and excluded.

teardowns.q: How much of this part can we actually promise?
teardowns.why: On hand minus demand, for every part at once — the BigQuery equivalent of Plex's own Sales Order Line Inventory Check screen. Which statuses count as demand is Plex's answer, not ours: it reads the Include_In_MRP flag. That design paid for itself within a day — when Jennilyn changed the flag in Plex, order demand fell from 508,807 units to 5,000 with no code change.
teardowns.watch: Job requirements are still missing — demand covers sales orders and BOM explosion, not what open jobs will consume.

teardowns.q: What is physically in the building?
teardowns.why: On-hand lives under the Part module, not Warehouse. Warehouse_v_Part_Quantity is the intuitive guess and does not exist on this tenant. Container statuses counted: OK, Hold, Inspection Required, Hold for Design Order.
teardowns.watch: Rework, lab analysis, defective and expired are deliberately excluded — a reworked container returns to normal inventory anyway, so counting it twice would inflate supply.

teardowns.q: What is all our stock worth in dollars?
teardowns.why: Confirmed 11 Sep: “Inventory Balance” on the revenue sheet means the dollar value of everything in inventory, raw materials through finished goods.
teardowns.watch: Returns 0 because Plex has costed nothing on this tenant. The source is not missing, it is unpopulated — an important distinction. Jennilyn is asking Justin where this should come from. Splitting into WIP / FG / Raw is separately impossible: no label lookup for the cost categories exists.

teardowns.q: How much counting did the warehouse do, and how right were they?
teardowns.why: Three numbers: locations counted, items counted, accuracy. Accuracy is a per-location hit rate — each assigned location either held what it should or it did not, and those yes/nos are averaged. Cycle counting lives under Part, not Warehouse — the same trap as on-hand inventory.
teardowns.watch: The first build weighted accuracy by quantity, which is better arithmetic and not what Vox means. Corrected. Counting is lumpy by design, so an empty month is normal — check locations_counted before showing a percentage or an idle month reads as 0% accurate.

teardowns.q: How much did each area actually make?
teardowns.why: One view covers every area — Blending, Bottling, Encapsulating, Labeling, Pre-Weigh, Preparation, Printing, Rework — rather than one view per line.
teardowns.watch: Plex says Encapsulating; the scorecard tile says “Encapsulation”. A goal typed with the tile's spelling never matches and shows 0% forever, with no error. This single mismatch is why every dropdown in the manual-data form reads its options from the reports.

teardowns.q: How much work is still on the floor?
teardowns.why: “Open” is the inverse of Completed / Cancelled / Hold. The original tile had no status filter at all and counted finished jobs as open work.

teardowns.q: What proportion came out right first time?
teardowns.why: Computed straight from production quantities — good ÷ total. Needs no quality records at all, which is why it works while the rest of Quality is empty.
teardowns.watch: DPMO divides by “opportunities per unit”, which is set to 1 as a placeholder nobody has defined. With 1, DPMO and defect rate are the same number wearing different labels. Sigma is deliberately not computed — a hand-rolled approximation risked being subtly wrong in cGMP-adjacent reporting.

teardowns.q: What did scrapped and reworked material cost us?
teardowns.why: Plex has no “Destroy” value — it calls destruction Scrap. That is why searching for a destruction field found nothing for weeks. Destroyed material is a nonconformance record whose final disposition is Scrap. The dollar figure is Plex's own Cost field, so it needs no external cost table.
teardowns.watch: Rework means two different things and the built one is not the one asked for. It is a disposition here and a container inventory status; Jennilyn named the container one. Different populations that will not agree. The container version needs a per-container cost.

teardowns.q: How long do quality problems take to close?
teardowns.why: Closed date minus problem date, per nonconformance, tagged with the month it closed so one view answers both “last month” and “rolling”.
teardowns.watch: Two open issues. The clock starts at Problem Date; if the existing Performance/Bonus standards were set against Entered Date, our number runs larger and looks like performance dropped on cutover day. And the standards themselves live in a table on the Monthly TAT sheet — they need to move into the form, with restricted edit access.

teardowns.q: What was approved to run outside spec?
teardowns.why: Richer than the sheet it replaces — correlates each deviation to job, part and work centre.
teardowns.watch: Deviation VALUE (pieces affected × part value) is not built: it needs a part cost, and Plex has costed nothing on this tenant. The first real deviation record arrived 11 Sep.

teardowns.q: What might we win?
teardowns.why: Quotes plus orders awaiting sales approval. This is the Plex half only — the full tile adds Monday.com, and that blend is by design, not a gap.
teardowns.watch: Opportunities and Forecast stages have no Plex source and never will — Plex tracks quotes and orders, never a deal before it becomes a quote. Those stay in Monday.

teardowns.q: How long since the last incident?
teardowns.why: Plex has no safety object of any kind. The manual-data form writes a dated incident log and the tile counts forward from the newest one.
teardowns.watch: An empty log reads as a perfect record, which is only true if the log is being kept. The form matters more than the tile.

teardowns.q: Which orders need artwork, and who do I ask about them?
teardowns.why: Not a scorecard tile — an operational queue that replaces a twice-daily manual loop (download from NetSuite, paste into a sheet, dedupe by hand, upload to Monday). Rebuilt from Jennilyn's own stored procedure with three additions: the rep name, an order-status filter of Pending Fulfillment, and a 14-day window. Dedupe is order number + customer part number, because dates change and an order can be cancelled and reopened.
teardowns.watch: Rows land in a holding board, never the live one, so notes and reason codes get reviewed first. Which rep is the “BDM” has never been stated, so both primary and secondary ship.

traps.title: Encapsulating vs “Encapsulation”
traps.body: Plex's work centre group is Encapsulating. The scorecard tile says “Encapsulation”. A goal typed the tile's way silently matches nothing and reads 0% forever.
traps.note: Every dropdown reads its options from the reports, so nobody types a scope by hand.

traps.title: Minimum Inventory Quantity
traps.body: Everyone says “minimum stock level”. No Plex field is called that. The field is Minimum_Inventory_Quantity.
traps.note: Confirmed 11 Sep. A value of 0 means “not assigned”, not “zero needed”.

traps.title: Scrap, not Destroy
traps.body: Plex has no destruction disposition. Destroyed material is scrapped.
traps.note: Weeks were spent looking for a field that was never going to exist.

traps.title: Part, not Warehouse
traps.body: On-hand inventory and cycle counting both live under the Part module. The Warehouse-named tables do not exist on this tenant.
traps.note: The general rule: when a warehouse-shaped concept comes back missing, look under Part before concluding Plex cannot do it.

traps.title: Revenue ≠ Sales
traps.body: Revenue counts goods shipped. Sales counts orders that reached Pending Fulfillment. They are deliberately different numbers and will not tie.
traps.note: This is why using one goal for both is an assumption worth confirming.

traps.title: Status names, not status keys
traps.body: Vox cut the sales-order status list from 10 to 7 and three numeric keys vanished. A report filtering a dead key returns 0 rows and looks like good news.
traps.note: All new report SQL matches on the status name.

traps.title: Test is not Production
traps.body: PlexTest resets periodically and the team enters practice data in it. PlexProd is empty until go-live.
traps.note: A figure read from test is true for that hour, not for the business.

risks.what: Revenue goals are the sales target
risks.why: No revenue-specific goal exists anywhere in BigQuery. The 12 loaded monthly figures are the company-wide sales target, which is measured against orders rather than shipments.
risks.where: Confirm or retract — one click in the form.

risks.what: Part costs do not exist yet
risks.why: Plex costs parts through Part_v_Snapshot, which holds no rows. Blocks Deviation $, container-based Rework $, and Inventory Balance.
risks.where: Product_Cost is not the fallback: 199 rows joining to 5 of 6,221 parts and none of the 33s.

risks.why: Nobody has defined opportunities per unit. Feeds the second heaviest-used source on the scorecard.
risks.where: A one-number change whenever Quality decides.

risks.why: We use Problem Date. If the standards were set against Entered Date, our figure runs consistently larger.
risks.where: Would look like a performance drop on the day we cut over.

risks.why: Built on the disposition; Jennilyn asked for the container status. They will not agree.
risks.where: Neither was silently chosen — both are documented.

risks.why: Quantity Available counts sales orders and BOM explosion, not what open jobs will consume.
risks.where: The job tables now hold real rows, so this is the next addition.

risks.why: No label lookup exists for the cost sub-types, so WIP / Finished Goods / Raw cannot be separated.
risks.where: Fine if the tile needs one grand total.
